analysis.one_liner: Replaces the graduated income tax with a flat 19% tax on wages and business income, ending taxes on capital gains, dividends, and estates.
analysis.headline: Senator Shelby's flat tax bill, introduced in March 2007 with three Republican cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current income tax code and replace it with one flat rate — 19%, dropping to 17% after 2009 — applied only to wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits. Investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed at all for individuals, and the estate tax would be repealed outright. Every income tax credit — including the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit — would be eliminated, along with the alternative minimum tax. The bill would also make it much harder to raise taxes later, requiring a three-fifths vote of either chamber to consider any tax increase.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households living on investment income gain the most: capital gains, dividends, and interest drop out of taxable income entirely, the estate and gift tax disappears, and the top wage rate falls from 35% to 19%. Large employers also gain new freedom over pension plans — contribution limits, nondiscrimination rules, and early-withdrawal penalties are all repealed, and companies could pull excess assets out of their pension funds and count them as income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: All individual income is taxed at a single 19% rate (17% after 2009) instead of graduated rates up to 35%, cutting taxes sharply for the highest earners [S2][S3].
Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation count as taxable income, so interest, dividends, capital gains, and rents owed by individuals are never taxed [S2][S3].
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes are repealed for deaths and gifts after 2007 [S2][S3].

A large standard deduction — $25,580 for joint filers plus $5,510 per dependent, inflation-adjusted — means many low-wage families owe no income tax, and the alternative minimum tax is repealed [S2][S3].

Pension rules limiting contributions, restricting distributions, and requiring plans to cover non-executive employees are repealed, and employers may reclaim excess pension assets without paying the excise tax [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working wage earners bear the burden. They lose every income tax credit, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit that supplement low wages, and their wages — unlike investment income — are taxed at the full flat rate. Because the plan taxes wages but not capital income and cuts the top rate from 35% to 19%, it shifts the overall tax burden toward people who work for a living and away from people who live off investments. The lost revenue would have to be made up by deficits or cuts to federal programs, and the bill's own three-fifths voting requirement would make it hard for a future Congress to raise rates back.

drawbacks.text: Every income tax credit is repealed, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit, which would raise effective taxes on many low- and middle-income working families even with the larger standard deduction [S2][S3].

Because taxable income consists only of wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits, a person whose income comes from capital gains, dividends, or interest would owe nothing on it, while a wage earner with the same income owes 19% [S2][S3].
The bill repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes outright, eliminating the only federal tax on very large inherited wealth [S2][S3].

It repeals pension nondiscrimination, minimum-coverage, and top-heavy rules that prevent plans from being designed solely for executives, and lets employers withdraw excess pension assets and pay income tax on them instead of the current reversion excise tax [S2][S3].

Section 201 locks in the flat structure by requiring a three-fifths vote in either chamber to consider any bill that raises a tax rate, cuts the standard deduction, or adds any credit or deduction — a rule that binds future majorities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Simplification is real: one rate, a big standard deduction, and no alternative minimum tax would make filing far easier for many households, and the generous deduction shields low-wage families entirely. But the core of the bill is a large tax cut for capital income and the wealthiest earners, paid for by wage earners who lose all their credits and by the Treasury, which would face a substantial revenue hole. The self-locking three-fifths rule makes the redistribution hard to undo. A well-designed flat tax would not exempt investment income while taxing wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the bill on March 29, 2007; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
Three Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 110th Congress, and it never reached the Senate floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary wage earners kept the existing progressive tax code, its tax credits, and the estate tax; the bill's intended beneficiaries — high earners, investors, and large estates — gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working people kept the existing tax code

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — the sponsor and all three cosponsors — while no Democrat cosponsored and the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee left the bill untouched.

industries.note: The bill untaxes capital gains, dividends, and interest entirely, cuts the top rate from 35% to 19%, and repeals the estate tax. The revenue those taxes raise would otherwise fund government programs or offset taxes on wages.

Repealing contribution limits, nondiscrimination, and minimum-coverage rules gives employers freedom to design plans around executives, and repealing the reversion excise tax lets them pull excess pension assets out of worker pension funds at only normal income-tax cost.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and governments as employers
industries.note: The bill imposes a 19% tax on employers, payable by nonprofit and government employers, on the value of noncash benefits they provide employees — including things like employer-provided health coverage.

Financial intermediation services would be taxed on the value of the services provided under special rules, while individuals' investment income goes untaxed — the net effect on the industry is genuinely mixed.
